{"id": "13:17/q01", "question": "What does 'from the sky' denote?", "turns_on": "How literally the source location is taken.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q01/p1", "position": "From the clouds or direction of the visible sky.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī note observation; Nasafī chooses clouds; Samarrāʾī lists clouds, rain, open space, or a roof as general Qurʾānic senses."}, {"id": "13:17/q01/p2", "position": "From the sky itself.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī allows it; Ālūsī cites reports without ruling on their authenticity and also mentions heavenly causes of vapor."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q02", "question": "What is the water sent down from the sky?", "turns_on": "The literal rain scene and its symbolic counterparts are both stated; inward authors differ on the gift it depicts.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q02/p1", "position": "The Qurʾān or revelation as the water represented.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Farrāʾ, Rāzī, and later authors compare its life-giving descent to rain; Elmalılı contrasts unacquired revelation with knowledge gained through work."}, {"id": "13:17/q02/p2", "position": "Rain, the literal scene.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn al-Jawzī and others say rain. Bayḍāwī allows clouds, the sky's direction, or the sky itself; Nasafī takes sky as clouds."}, {"id": "13:17/q02/p3", "position": "Divine gifts, knowledge, light, love, or disclosure in inward readings.", "reasons": "Sulamī reports light, gifts, shyness, and certainty; Qāshānī has Holy Spirit knowledge; Bursevī's Najmī source distinguishes soul, heart, and secret; Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes divine outpouring measured by recipients."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q03", "question": "How can the valleys be said to flow?", "turns_on": "Whether wādī here is the channel or the water in it.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q03/p1", "position": "The waters of the valleys flowed; the container stands for its contents or 'waters' is omitted.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī and Ibn al-Jawzī supply the genitive; Jurjānī calls attribution to the ravines a figure in the predication; Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares a flowing waterspout."}, {"id": "13:17/q03/p2", "position": "Wādī can itself mean flowing water, making the predication literal.", "reasons": "Qurtubī and Ālūsī record this sense."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q04", "question": "What are the valleys?", "turns_on": "The word can name a physical channel or, by extension, its flowing contents.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q04/p1", "position": "Low channels or hollows where rainwater gathers and flows.", "reasons": "Most linguists say open ground between mountains or at their foot; Jishumī and Ṭabrisī mention the diya etymology; Ibn ʿĀshūr says a broad extended hollow; Asad calls it a normally dry riverbed."}, {"id": "13:17/q04/p2", "position": "Awdiyah is the plural of wādin, with an unusual broken-plural pattern.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī derives it by overlap of fāʿil and faʿīl patterns; andiya is offered as parallel; al-Samīn counters a claim of uniqueness with jāʾiz/ajwiza and nāḥiya/anḥiya."}, {"id": "13:17/q04/p3", "position": "The flowing water itself by extension.", "reasons": "Shammar, Bayḍāwī, Qurtubī, and Ālūsī permit naming the water for its channel; Abū ʿAlī instead supplies the omitted 'waters of the valleys'."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q05", "question": "Why are the valleys indefinite?", "turns_on": "The notes offer complementary effects of indefiniteness.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q05/p1", "position": "Rain falls in different regions at different times, so only some valleys flow.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Ālūsī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Asad give this explanation; Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds differences of length, breadth, and capacity."}, {"id": "13:17/q05/p2", "position": "The plural evokes valleys of differing sizes and receptivity.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī points to size, length, breadth, and capacity."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q06", "question": "What does 'according to its measure' measure?", "turns_on": "Whether qadr relates to the valley's size, a divinely fixed beneficial allotment, or its water volume.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q06/p1", "position": "Each valley's physical capacity or size; small takes little and large much.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Qutayba, and many later authors use this account; Rāzī describes overflow; Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses nondestructive fit."}, {"id": "13:17/q06/p2", "position": "The amount God apportioned in wisdom, particularly what benefits without harm.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Māwardī give the allotment; Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Ālūsī, and Abū Ḥayyān connect it to beneficial rain rather than destructive excess; Ālūsī says it need not reach the rim."}, {"id": "13:17/q06/p3", "position": "The measure of each valley's water, by shifted reference of the suffix.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī rejects measuring valleys against themselves; Zarkashī gives this wording, and Ālūsī reports its grammatical basis."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q07", "question": "How is bi-qadariha read?", "turns_on": "Vocalization of the dāl; the notes generally retain the same sense.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q07/p1", "position": "With sukūn on dāl, bi-qadriha.", "reasons": "Reported for al-Ḥasan, al-Ashhab, Zayd b. ʿAlī, Abū ʿAmr in one transmission, and others; Ṭabrisī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī call the forms dialectal and equivalent."}, {"id": "13:17/q07/p2", "position": "With fatḥa on dāl, bi-qadariha.", "reasons": "The majority reading is reported by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q08", "question": "What does qadr mean here as a word?", "turns_on": "The noun's measure sense and its verbal-noun sense support different construals of the phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q08/p1", "position": "Amount or proportion measured in relation to a thing.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī cites quantities by weight; Ṭabrisī contrasts exact proportion with weight admitting excess or deficiency; Biqāʿī uses proportion without excess; Ibn ʿĀshūr says measurement."}, {"id": "13:17/q08/p2", "position": "An apportioning, a verbal noun for what God determines.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Zajjāj explain the measured filling as God's assignment."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q09", "question": "What is the grammatical relation of bi-qadariha?", "turns_on": "The phrase's grammatical attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q09/p1", "position": "It modifies or depends on sālat, describing how the valleys flowed.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥawfī gives the attachment; al-Samīn and Ālūsī report it."}, {"id": "13:17/q09/p2", "position": "It is an adjective or circumstantial qualifier of awdiya.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ calls it an adjective; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a ḥāl; al-Samīn reports the option."}, {"id": "13:17/q09/p3", "position": "It depends on anzala.", "reasons": "Ālūsī mentions this third parse."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q10", "question": "What is al-sayl and why is it definite?", "turns_on": "Whether al-sayl resumes an implied event or denotes the resulting water.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q10/p1", "position": "The torrent or flowing water, made definite by the preceding 'flowed'.", "reasons": "Jishumī says sayl is both event noun and the water; Abū Ḥayyān says the verb introduces its verbal noun, which al-sayl resumes; Ālūsī records an objection that event and concrete torrent differ, then leaves the event sense open."}, {"id": "13:17/q10/p2", "position": "The flowing event itself, originally a verbal noun.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib as quoted by Ālūsī cites its verbal-noun origin."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q11", "question": "What does 'the flood carried' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q11/p1", "position": "The torrent lifted and carried its load.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī explains iḥtimāl as carrying with strength; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and Ālūsī say iftaʿala has the simple ḥamala sense, comparing iqtidara/qadara."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q12", "question": "What is the flood's zabad?", "turns_on": "Physical foam is the vehicle; sources vary in the particular spiritual or doctrinal residue it depicts.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q12/p1", "position": "Froth, scum, bubbles, and flood debris churned up and carried above water.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Zajjāj, Jishumī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī describe it; poetry about a river or Euphrates is cited. Al-Samīn also notes milk foam, sea foam, and a proverb of abundance."}, {"id": "13:17/q12/p2", "position": "Doubt, disbelief, falsehood, satanic suggestions, or egoistic thoughts in the comparison.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās identifies doubt and unbelief; Burhān lists doubts and desires; Nasafī and Bursevī report whispers; Biqāʿī includes idol worship and polemic; the inward readings identify self-regard."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q13", "question": "What does rābiyan describe?", "turns_on": "The lexical glosses are compatible; the rhetorical question is why the height is stressed.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q13/p1", "position": "High, swollen, or floating above the water.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda derives it from rabā 'to grow'; Ṭabarī cites 22:5 and rabwa, a mound; Rāzī records Zajjāj's height and another's swelling as close explanations."}, {"id": "13:17/q13/p2", "position": "It emphasizes foam's apparent dominance without any lasting substance.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Biqāʿī, and Ālūsī explain that height makes falsehood appear to prevail; Ālūsī prefers 'swollen' over 'above it' so the foam's rise seems inherent."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q14", "question": "What do rain and valleys represent in the parable?", "turns_on": "Different versions identify the descending gift and the recipients' faculty more narrowly; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān dispute the symbolic report's attribution.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q14/p1", "position": "Qurʾānic guidance or truth enters human hearts according to their receptivity.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Farrāʾ, Wāḥidī, Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr and many later sources use this correspondence; capacities reflect certainty, understanding, purity, intelligence, belief,

 or works."}, {"id": "13:17/q14/p2", "position": "The water is revealed law, and intelligent and foolish hearts each receive a share.", "reasons": "Attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān; both question its transmission and resist abandoning ordinary Arabic without cause, but allow a charitable sense if authentic."}, {"id": "13:17/q14/p3", "position": "The valleys can stand for people's minds.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUyayna says each mind carries the Qurʾān according to capacity."}, {"id": "13:17/q14/p4", "position": "The water signifies faith or truth and the valleys believers' hearts.", "reasons": "The author of al-Naẓm gives faith and truth; Wāḥidī's other authorities call it guidance."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q15", "question": "How is the kindling verb read?", "turns_on": "Person of the prefix, with contextual support from the earlier address or following third-person 'people'.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q15/p1", "position": "Third person yuqīdūn, 'they kindle'.", "reasons": "Hamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ, Khalaf, Kufans and other readers are listed. Abū ʿUbayd prefers it because 'what benefits people' follows without direct address; the subject can be people generally or the associaters."}, {"id": "13:17/q15/p2", "position": "Second person tūqidūn, 'you kindle'.", "reasons": "The other readers, including many of the Seven, read tāʾ. It continues the address of 13:16 or addresses people generally; Qiraat-Er says it makes listeners the workers."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q16", "question": "What is heated over the fire?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q16/p1", "position": "Metals or ores, especially gold and silver for adornment and iron, copper, brass, lead, or tin for tools.", "reasons": "Mujāhid names iron, copper, lead; the wider lists differ slightly. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes crucible smelting; Zamakhsharī notes iron's strength; metalwork throws off impurity."}, {"id": "13:17/q16/p2", "position": "Material kindled for useful goods, with 'fire' describing the actual melting.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Baghawī gloss iqād as kindling so the material melts; Ṭabrisī gives related verbal forms."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q17", "question": "How does 'in the fire' attach?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase gives a distinct location, describes the object's state, or reinforces the action.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q17/p1", "position": "It attaches to 'they kindle'.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī and al-Ḥawfī support it because clay can be heated without itself entering flame (28:38); Abū Ḥayyān allows emphatic redundancy, like flying with wings (6:38)."}, {"id": "13:17/q17/p2", "position": "It is an omitted circumstantial participle, 'while it is in the fire'.", "reasons": "Makkī, the Basran scholar in Ṭabrisī, Qurtubī, Nasafī, and Ālūsī treat it as state of the object; what is kindled is already in fire, so direct attachment is challenged."}, {"id": "13:17/q17/p3", "position": "It emphasizes intense work of melting.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this rhetorical reading."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q18", "question": "How does 'seeking adornment or goods' function grammatically?", "turns_on": "Purpose object versus circumstantial verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q18/p1", "position": "A purpose accusative: they kindle in order to obtain these goods.", "reasons": "Qurtubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, Ālūsī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr prefer this; it makes the metal's benefit explicit."}, {"id": "13:17/q18/p2", "position": "A circumstantial verbal noun: kindling while seeking them.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī's Basran source and al-Ḥawfī give this parse; al-Samīn records it as less likely."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q19", "question": "What is ḥilya?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q19/p1", "position": "Ornaments or jewelry worn for adornment, typically of gold and silver.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Māwardī, Ṭabrisī, Qurtubī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and others specify wearable ornament; Biqāʿī gives bracelets and rings."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q20", "question": "What is matāʿ here?", "turns_on": "The verse's metal goods are a contextual instance of a broader Arabic word.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q20/p1", "position": "Useful goods, implements, vessels, or articles made from metal.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Zajjāj, Māwardī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and others cite iron, copper, brass, or lead vessels and tools; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes coined precious metal."}, {"id": "13:17/q20/p2", "position": "Anything enjoyed or used, a general benefit.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda cites al-Mushaʿath's verse; Ṭabarī and Wāḥidī repeat it. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ distinguishes broad matāʿ from household athāth across cited verses; Ibn Qutayba also notes duration and divorced women's provision."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q21", "question": "What kind of foam comes from fired material?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q21/p1", "position": "Dross, slag, or separated impurities that rise from molten metal like flood foam.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Qatāda, Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn Kathīr, and many others explain the purification; Wāḥidī mentions bellows expelling some, and Ibn ʿĀshūr crucibles."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q22", "question": "What does min in 'from what they kindle' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether min marks the foam's source or a part of the material.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q22/p1", "position": "Origin or source: foam arises from the metal.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, al-Samīn, and Ālūsī allow or prefer this; Ālūsī says it better preserves the parable's structure."}, {"id": "13:17/q22/p2", "position": "Partitive: some of the heated material becomes foam.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān prefers this because the foam is part of the metal; Ibn ʿĀshūr says min is partitive in origin. Some careful scholars in Ālūsī object that it disrupts the analogy."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q23", "question": "How is 'there is foam like it' parsed?", "turns_on": "Function of mithluhu and whether the preceding phrase supplies the predicate.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q23/p1", "position": "Zabad is subject, mithluhu its adjective, and the fronted prepositional phrase its predicate.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Nasafī, al-Samīn, and Ālūsī give this parse; Sibawayh is reported for it."}, {"id": "13:17/q23/p2", "position": "Zabad is subject and mithluhu its predicate.", "reasons": "Qurtubī reports this alternative."}, {"id": "13:17/q23/p3", "position": "Zabad is raised by the adverbial expression.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī attributes this to al-Akhfash."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q24", "question": "Why describe the metals indirectly as what is heated?", "turns_on": "The notes offer overlapping explanations of why the materials are described by their treatment and purpose.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q24/p1", "position": "The description covers all metals and treats prized materials as insignificant before God.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī compares 28:38; Bayḍāwī and Biqāʿī repeat the royal-disdain explanation. Ālūsī defends it against the claim it conflicts with metal's usefulness."}, {"id": "13:17/q24/p2", "position": "The ornament/utility pair displays both metal's benefits and the full range of metalwork.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Biqāʿī, and Abū Ḥayyān say both categories of use are named, enabling the later generalization about benefit."}, {"id": "13:17/q24/p3", "position": "It is concise and keeps the process producing foam in view.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says explicitly naming gold and silver would require a longer description; their omission also counters fascination with them."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q25", "question": "What does 'God strikes truth and falsehood' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether yadribu directly establishes the two terms or requires an implicit 'parable of'.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q25/p1", "position": "God sets forth the likeness of truth and falsehood, with 'likeness' or its preposition omitted.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, al-Naẓm, Abū Ḥayyān, Ālūsī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr supply an implicit comparison; Ālūsī says the omission makes image and referent seem identical."}, {"id": "13:17/q25/p2", "position": "God establishes truth and falsehood in the parable, without omitted wording.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers the ordinary force of ḍaraba as fixing something, like driving a peg; he rejects added 'likeness' as unsupported and unnecessary in view of the final mention of parables."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q26", "question": "How do the images map onto truth and falsehood?", "turns_on": "The shared contrast is benefit and endurance against apparent height and disappearance; sources differ in the precise religious referents.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q26/p1", "position": "Useful, lasting water and refined metal are truth, faith, guidance, or righteous deeds; transient foam and dross are falsehood, disbelief, doubt, or evil deeds.", "reasons": "This is the dominant mapping from Muqātil through Study Quran. Ibn Qutayba and Wāḥidī emphasize falsehood's temporary height; Ibn ʿAbbās connects the result to judgment and righteous action; Ibn ʿĀshūr makes it promise and warning."}, {"id": "13:17/q26/p2", "position": "Believers and their conviction are the enduring substance; unbelievers and their party resemble foam.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī states the person-level map; Baghawī calls it consolation for believers; Ibn al-Jawzī and ʿAṭāʾ report it; Ibn ʿĀshūr foresees polytheists' destruction and believers' survival."}, {"id": "13:17/q26/p3", "position": "Rain and fire map divine revelation and humanly acquired true knowledge, respectively.", "reasons": "Elmalılı distinguishes water descending without effort from refined knowledge gained through work, while both are divine gifts."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q27", "question": "What does jufāʾ mean?", "turns_on": "The word is explained through physical expulsion, drying or congealing, and scattering; these accounts all explain its loss.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q27/p1", "position": "Cast off, discarded foam or debris swept to banks, trees, or a pot's rim.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Farrāʾ
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

, Ṭabarī, Zajjāj, Qatāda, Jishumī and many others cite valleys and boiling pots expelling froth; Ibn Fāris ties the root to repudiation."}, {"id": "13:17/q27/p2", "position": "Dispersed and carried away by wind, like a cloud broken apart.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbārī cites jafaʾat al-rīḥ al-saḥāb; Thaʿlabī, Māwardī, Baghawī, Biqāʿī, and Ālūsī report it."}, {"id": "13:17/q27/p3", "position": "Dried, congealed, or clinging matter that has lost use.", "reasons": "Muqātil says dried useless foam; Ibn Jurayj and Mujāhid say frozen or solid; Qatāda says it sticks to trees; Basran grammarians relate it to drying and absorption."}, {"id": "13:17/q27/p4", "position": "Gone, dissolved, and without substance or benefit.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Biqāʿī gloss it as disintegrating; Ibn ʿAbbās says foam amounts to nothing on touch; al-Rummānī explains perishing after remaining in place."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q28", "question": "How is jufāʾ formed and read?", "turns_on": "Whether the hamza is radical or substituted, and whether Ruʾba's lām variant is admissible.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q28/p1", "position": "Ruʾba's jafālan or ajfal with lām.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and later authorities report Ruʾba's form from wind scattering clouds. Abū Ḥātim rejects Bedouin readings and disparages him; al-Samīn replies that Zamakhsharī praised his eloquence."}, {"id": "13:17/q28/p2", "position": "Jufāʾ, with original hamza; its pattern can be a verbal or collective noun.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ compares ghuthāʾ and other gathered debris; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it a verbal noun; al-Samīn prefers radical hamza over a replacement of wāw."}, {"id": "13:17/q28/p3", "position": "The hamza replaces an original wāw.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ's alternative is reported by al-Samīn, who rejects it because the root with wāw does not fit the meaning."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q29", "question": "How is jufāʾ parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q29/p1", "position": "A circumstantial accusative describing the foam as it departs.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, Zajjāj, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Ālūsī agree; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the word a verbal noun used thus."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q30", "question": "What other lexical families are compared with jufāʾ?", "turns_on": "Biqāʿī's proposed connections extend beyond the verse word's immediate lexical gloss.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q30/p1", "position": "The j-f-ʾ family centers on casting away and separation.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī tracks expelling foam, throwing a person down, uprooting plants, vacating a ship, and coarse nonadherence."}, {"id": "13:17/q30/p2", "position": "Inverted related roots describe hollow receptacles, sudden arrival, movement, and separation.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī discusses jawf, f-j-ʾ, a swift messenger, detached groups, spreading scent, and restless animals."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q31", "question": "Why mention foam before what remains?", "turns_on": "The sources give different reasons for the summary's sequence and emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q31/p1", "position": "Foam was mentioned last and falsehood is the later term, so the exposition follows the near item.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān observes reverse-order exposition and cites 3:106 as another example; he admits first-mentioned order can also be eloquent."}, {"id": "13:17/q31/p2", "position": "What disappears is removed first, then the survivor is counted.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this explanation."}, {"id": "13:17/q31/p3", "position": "Foam is immediately visible, whereas useful substance persists afterward.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this as gathering then division."}, {"id": "13:17/q31/p4", "position": "The faʾ and ammā emphasize the conclusion and its warning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the clause branches from the torrent's foam and draws attention to promise and warning."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q32", "question": "How is the surface foam's disappearance contrasted with the enduring benefit?", "turns_on": "The text's implicit and sequential relationships.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q32/p1", "position": "The water scene leaves clear water under the scum, unstated but understood.", "reasons": "Asad supplies the ellipsis; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the paired contrast with metal is left unstated because readily understood."}, {"id": "13:17/q32/p2", "position": "The sequential fāʾs unfold the scene and support both a whole-scene and component comparison.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies the consequences of descending rain and sees eloquence in the staged sequence."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q33", "question": "What remains and benefits people?", "turns_on": "Whether the immediate referent includes both water and metal, water alone, or their moral counterparts.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q33/p1", "position": "Clear water and purified metals, useful for drink, crops, tools, ornament, or exchange.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ṭabarī, Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, al-Ālūsī and others include both substances; water gathers, seeps to wells, springs, and crops while metal is fashioned and kept."}, {"id": "13:17/q33/p2", "position": "Certainty, guidance, good deeds, useful knowledge, truth, and pure virtues in the moral analogy.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās identifies certainty and good deeds; Sulamī says sincere states and bestowed certainty; Qāshānī says pure virtues; Ṭabāṭabāʾī makes benefit a defining sign of truth."}, {"id": "13:17/q33/p3", "position": "Pure water alone, or its growth and pasture.", "reasons": "Mujāhid says clear water; Wāḥidī notes vegetation; ʿAwf mentions drinking and crops. The wider metal comparison is then implied."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q34", "question": "What is 'the earth' where benefit remains?", "turns_on": "Literal ground, inward heart, or the specific courtyard in Damghānī's report.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q34/p1", "position": "The literal earth, including reservoirs, springs, crops, or human possession upon it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī includes water in ground and metals possessed by earth's people; Bayḍāwī notes springs and wells."}, {"id": "13:17/q34/p2", "position": "The heart or soul as the receiving ground.", "reasons": "Damghānī and Muqātil name hearts; Qāshānī names soul; Ibn al-Jawzī transmits this metaphor."}, {"id": "13:17/q34/p3", "position": "The courtyard of the congregational mosque.", "reasons": "Damghānī reports Mujāhid for this unusual gloss."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q35", "question": "What is the force of 'remains'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q35/p1", "position": "It stays in place over time and thus continues to benefit.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī gives makatha, mukitha, tamakkatha; Damghānī stresses benefit, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī transmits the morphological variants."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q36", "question": "What does 'God sets forth parables' add?", "turns_on": "How broadly the final demonstrative and plural 'parables' are taken.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q36/p1", "position": "God makes difficult moral truths clear through familiar images and invites reflection.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī says parables circulate through lands; Bayḍāwī and Bursevī stress explanation of obscure matters; Ibn Kathīr cites 29:43 and a report about weeping if one failed to understand a parable; Biqāʿī praises its clarity."}, {"id": "13:17/q36/p2", "position": "The ending is a general coda, reaffirming this instance and closing before the next verse.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the general includes the particular; Qurtubī says the sentence closes here; Ṭabrisī reports an alternative boundary at the next sentence."}, {"id": "13:17/q36/p3", "position": "The demonstrative can point to visible natural events as signs of unseen realities.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this option, which differs from taking it as pointing back to the narrated parable."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q37", "question": "How does Arabic use 'parable' or mathal in cited examples?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q37/p1", "position": "Mathal can be a description or an illustrative saying circulated among people.", "reasons": "Damghānī cites believer and Paradise descriptions (29:43, 59:21, 47:15, 13:35); Ṭabrisī says striking a parable makes it travel among people."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q38", "question": "How many parables are in the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether independently introduced physical images count as separate parables or as instances in a single comparison.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q38/p1", "position": "Two: floodwater with foam, then metal with dross.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and Study Quran mark the second at the fire clause; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it makes the lesson familiar to Meccan goldsmiths."}, {"id": "13:17/q38/p2", "position": "Three examples within one parable.", "reasons": "Qatāda counts foam disappearing, water enduring, and metal being refined; Ṭabrisī and Zarkashī transmit this count; Muqātil says three examples together."}, {"id": "13:17/q38/p3", "position": "One unfolding parable with several instances.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects both two and three, observing that the two kinds of foam are reunited in the one conclusion."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q39", "question": "How does this verse link to its neighbors and the sūra?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is read chiefly against the immediately preceding proof, later outcomes, or parallel Qurʾānic images.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q39/p1", "position": "It follows 13:16's proof of divine oneness and blind/sighted and darkness/light contrast, then promises truth's victory.", "reasons": "Zajjāj, Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Iṣlāḥī make the link; Biqāʿī ties revelation to the sūra's thunder/rain theme; Ibn ʿĀshūr reads warning and glad tidings into the next verse."}, {"id": "13:17/q39/p2", "position": "It parallels other rain, fire, mirage, and light comparisons in the Qurʾān.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites 2:17, 2:19 and 24:39-40; Ibn ʿĀshūr also cites 2:19. Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites verses

 on truth overcoming falsehood."}, {"id": "13:17/q39/p3", "position": "The next clause begins with those who answer their Lord.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī reports al-Ḥasan and al-Balkhī treating the parable phrase as the end of this passage."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q40", "question": "Which Prophetic reports illuminate the rain and refinement imagery?", "turns_on": "These are distinct reports and analogies; no single report is made the occasion of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q40/p1", "position": "The Prophet's guidance and knowledge are like rain falling on three kinds of soil.", "reasons": "A sound report in Abū Ḥayyān and Zarkashī, both Ṣaḥīḥ collections in Ibn Kathīr, and ungraded quotations in Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguish fertile, water-retaining, and barren ground."}, {"id": "13:17/q40/p2", "position": "Other reports compare seekers of water, moths rushing into fire, or sins to sea foam.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr quotes the Jewish mirage report at resurrection and the Prophet's fire-and-moths analogy; al-Samīn cites a sea-foam forgiveness report."}, {"id": "13:17/q40/p3", "position": "Bellows or fire remove dross from iron.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the image without a chain or grading."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q41", "question": "What does the parable teach about truth's permanence?", "turns_on": "The general victory claim is elaborated either as a rule of history, a criterion of reality, or a rule of measured divine giving.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q41/p1", "position": "Truth endures and benefits while falsehood temporarily appears high and then vanishes by God's practice.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Ibn ʿAbbās, Biqāʿī, Iṣlāḥī, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī use the physical processes to explain lasting truth, judgment, and the eventual triumph of its people; Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 17:81 and 21:18."}, {"id": "13:17/q41/p2", "position": "Truth is what matches reality or fulfills its end; falsehood lacks stability when examined.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī quotes al-Rāghib and develops the distinction for statements, acts, beliefs, and dependent beings; true realities cooperate toward God's ends, whereas defects frustrate them."}, {"id": "13:17/q41/p3", "position": "Recipients measure divine gift, yet their capacities remain subject to God.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 15:21, 39:6, 11:123 and 13:31, then says transient impurities emerge while mercy persists."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q42", "question": "How do inward readings map the water, fire, and their foam?", "turns_on": "The inward sources differ over the divine influx, the faculty receiving it, and the impurity removed.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q42/p1", "position": "Qurʾān and faith refine hearts; whispers, ostentation, laziness, and spiritual defects are the foam.", "reasons": "Nasafī's majority reading makes adornment noble states and morals, goods sincere deeds; Qurtubī reports virtues as ornaments; Bursevī cites al-Kāshifī and Abū al-Layth."}, {"id": "13:17/q42/p2", "position": "Divine light or gifts cleanse receptive hearts, leaving sincere states and certainty.", "reasons": "Sulamī reports al-Wāsiṭī's shy pearl and Qurʾānic generosity, Ibn ʿAṭāʾ's light removing heedlessness, and another account of guidance, gnosis, love, longing, and witnessing."}, {"id": "13:17/q42/p3", "position": "Knowledge from the Holy Spirit floods heart valleys; love's fire refines gnosis and virtues; conceit is the foam.", "reasons": "Qāshānī maps the two processes to knowledge and love, with the soul's admiration and veiling dispersed while pure meanings remain; he cites 8:11."}, {"id": "13:17/q42/p4", "position": "Love, beauty, and disclosure water successive levels of soul, heart, and secret.", "reasons": "Bursevī's Najmī commentary pairs them with animal traits, spiritual selfhood, and figurative existence as three foams; the Mathnawī says eternal qualities burn transient ones."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q43", "question": "What do cited Arabic examples say about vowel shortening?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q43/p1", "position": "Long kasra and damma may be clipped while retaining movement; accusative fatḥa behaves differently.", "reasons": "Sībawayh adduces articulation of nūn in min maʾmanik, dialectal faḵḏ and ʿaḍud, an informant-confirmed rajaz form ṣāḥibī, and Imruʾ al-Qays on partial rounding; accusative is excluded."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q44", "question": "What general Arabic syntax is cited around the verse?", "turns_on": "These are separate grammatical examples in the supplied notes, some only indirectly pertinent to the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q44/p1", "position": "Short masculine names decline, while annexation or definiteness changes diptote case; feminine-looking name endings require analysis.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares proper names, diminutives, bint and ukht, hinta, and ḍarbat; the forms follow their built patterns."}, {"id": "13:17/q44/p2", "position": "An/inna clauses can occupy noun slots, start fresh statements, or express causal and emphatic senses.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares verbs of thought, law/lawlā, mudh, ammā, oath, thumma, and aʾī; al-Khalīl's readings are included, with examples from 17:100 and 20:119."}, {"id": "13:17/q44/p3", "position": "Locative and temporal expressions may be accusative adverbials or nominative equivalents of a predicate.", "reasons": "Sībawayh adduces Abū Dhuʾayb, al-Aḥwaṣ, Ibn Ḥurma on daraj al-sayl, distances, time, and Yunus from Abū ʿAmr; the construction is restricted by attested usage."}, {"id": "13:17/q44/p4", "position": "Fixed truth/falsehood formulas and comparison or measure nouns have special accusative specifications.", "reasons": "Sībawayh reports al-Khalīl on lā qawlak, the definite al-batta, and the variable al-ḥaqq/al-bāṭil, then discusses omitted min, measures, and poetic accusatives."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q45", "question": "What general Arabic rhetoric is cited around the verse?", "turns_on": "The cited rhetoric distinguishes figures of comparison, attribution, and evaluative naming.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q45/p1", "position": "Metaphors transfer visible qualities to intellectual ones or move the figure into predication.", "reasons": "Jurjānī uses light for proof, faith, and knowledge, darkness for doubt, a balance for justice, and jāḥiẓ's strainer; his Dalāʾil analysis locates the figure in attribution, including ravines flowing."}, {"id": "13:17/q45/p2", "position": "Arabic permits ellipsis, repetition, number shifts, changes of address, fronting, and related predication.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda lists singular/plural and dual patterns, human-like reporting of nonhuman things, omitted predicates, added letters, and accepted Arabic usage; he rejects alleged foreign origins of Ṭā Hā and sijjīl."}, {"id": "13:17/q45/p3", "position": "Remote similes require finding an unexpected shared feature; imaginative analogies may persuade without literally proving causation.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī contrasts immediate sun/mirror imagery with a paralytic's mirror, lightning/finger, book/branches, and Abū Tammām's flood or gray-hair conceits."}, {"id": "13:17/q45/p4", "position": "Some seeming metaphors deny a claim to full existence or value; others assert likeness.", "reasons": "Jurjānī distinguishes calling ignorance death or spent wealth present from comparing a hard question with death."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q46", "question": "What names and descriptions of the Qurʾān are supplied?", "turns_on": "The supplied etymologies vary, while the functional names emphasize different effects of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q46/p1", "position": "Furqān names its separation of truth from falsehood; Kitāb, Dhikr, and other names name other functions.", "reasons": "Māwardī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Suyūṭī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr explain Furqān, Book, Reminder, Light, Guidance, Healing, Rope, Straight Path, Wisdom, al-Muhaymin, and Tanzīl; some Sufis give Furqān a distinction/union sense."}, {"id": "13:17/q46/p2", "position": "Qurʾān is linked to recitation or to gathering; sources disagree over the better derivation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers recitation, citing Ḥassān; Qatāda, Abū ʿUbayda, and others cite gathering and poetry about a womb; Ibn ʿĀshūr derives it from reading and rejects a proposed plural from qarina."}, {"id": "13:17/q46/p3", "position": "Sūra may derive from a building section, a rank, or a remainder, with hamza and plural vowels varying.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn ʿAṭiyya cite al-Nābigha and al-Aʿshā; Qurʾānic suwar has open wāw, building sūr a still wāw."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q47", "question": "How was the Qurʾān collected according to cited reports?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on timing, the named keeper of verses, the scribes, and disposal of codices.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q47/p1", "position": "It was memorized and written under the Prophet, then Abū Bakr commissioned Zayd after the deaths at Yamāma.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Itqān report palm stalks, stones, shoulder blades, memory, ʿUmar's urgency, and Zayd's gathering; al-Bayhaqī distinguishes ordering verses in their sūras in the Prophet's presence."}, {"id": "13:17/q47/p2", "position": "A missing ending of Barāʾa was found with Khuzayma or Abū Khuzayma, in the first or second collection.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the first collection against Ṭabarī and notes Bukhārī's name Abū Khuzayma; al-Itqān reports Abū Khuzayma, while another Aḥzāb verse was found with Khuzayma in the second."}, {"id": "13:17/q47/p3", "position": "ʿUthmān used Ḥafṣa's sheets and regional copies, directed Qurayshī language, and removed other codices.", "reasons": "Reports differ on the assisting scribes (three named Qurayshīs versus Abān alone) and whether remaining codices were burned, torn, or buried; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects Abān-alone and prefers burning/tearing."}, {"id": "13:17/q47/p4", "position": "Al-Itqān reports ʿAlī also gathered the text after the Prophet's death.", "reasons": "Ibn Sīrīn transmits ʿAlī's vow to

 remain home except for Friday prayer until completion."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q48", "question": "How is Qurʾānic inimitability argued in the cited material?", "turns_on": "The minimum challenged unit and how its miraculous character is known.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q48/p1", "position": "Qurʾānic composition remains clear and consistent beyond imitable poetic devices.", "reasons": "Bāqillānī contrasts crafted horse similes and antithesis with the Qurʾān's sustained order; Ibn ʿAṭiyya praises its eloquence; Samarrāʾī stresses deliberate artistry."}, {"id": "13:17/q48/p2", "position": "A complete sūra, or an equal length, is the minimum proven inimitable unit.", "reasons": "Al-Ashʿarī and most Ashʿarites hold this, citing even al-Kawthar; Bāqillānī says Arab inability and the challenge to all sūras prove it and prefers this route over designation."}, {"id": "13:17/q48/p3", "position": "Each sūra is independently inimitable; some Muʿtazilites set a longer-verse or many-verse threshold.", "reasons": "Bāqillānī and Zarkashī report these variants; the dispute turns on what the challenge proves below a full sūra."}, {"id": "13:17/q48/p4", "position": "Miraculous status could be known by authoritative designation.", "reasons": "A senior authority proposes it; Bāqillānī and Zarkashī favor Arab incapacity as the stronger demonstration."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q49", "question": "What general reading practices appear in the cited material?", "turns_on": "These are general reading notes supplied alongside the verse-specific variants.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q49/p1", "position": "Abū ʿAmr's reading is transmitted through early readers and characterized as easy and light.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid reports routes through Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ubayy, and others, with a contested attribution to Naṣr b. ʿĀṣim; he notes Basran adoption."}, {"id": "13:17/q49/p2", "position": "Pausing or joining between sūras follows rules of completion, basmala, and repeated sūra.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī prefers pause at a sūra's end while allowing other methods and gives exceptions for Tawba and repetition."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q50", "question": "What other reports about reward, wrongdoing, or judgment are cited?", "turns_on": "These are separate transmitted narratives in the supplied corpus.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q50/p1", "position": "A slave's stolen cloak and another man's sandal straps bring a warning of hellfire.", "reasons": "Ibn Hishām reports Abū Hurayra's Khaybar-return account, naming Rifāʿa b. Zayd and the stray arrow."}, {"id": "13:17/q50/p2", "position": "Paradise's date palms have jeweled trunks and branches, clothing leaves, and abundant seedless fruit.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba reports Ibn ʿAbbās's description, including milk-white, honey-sweet, butter-soft fruit."}, {"id": "13:17/q50/p3", "position": "A letter during ʿAlī's siege pleads for aid before the sender is torn apart.", "reasons": "Bāqillānī transmits the letter's urgent wording."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q51", "question": "How do thoughts and heart states arise in the cited psychological account?", "turns_on": "The account moves from mental causes to their ultimate cause, which Rāzī says remains insufficiently explained.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q51/p1", "position": "The heart receives sensory and inner effects; thoughts arise, move intention, and end in action.", "reasons": "Rāzī summarizes al-Ghazālī's heart as enclosure, target, mirror, and basin; imagination, appetite, anger, and temperament supply effects; harmful thoughts are whispers, beneficial ones inspiration."}, {"id": "13:17/q51/p2", "position": "The chain of created thoughts must end in the Necessary Existent, though the explanation needs refinement.", "reasons": "Rāzī adds an anti-regress argument and judges al-Ghazālī's account incomplete."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q52", "question": "What happens to the recitation of the stoning verse in the cited reports?", "turns_on": "Different explanations of why a recited text was not entered in the codex.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q52/p1", "position": "Its recitation was lifted while the ruling remained, perhaps to avoid displaying a severe law or because of dispute.", "reasons": "Ibn Ḥajar offers the apparent-sense and disagreement accounts; Suyūṭī suggests easing the community and encouraging concealment."}, {"id": "13:17/q52/p2", "position": "Zayd and ʿUmar report requests or proposals to write the verse but no entry in the codex.", "reasons": "Al-Nasāʾī and Ibn al-Durays report the exchanges; Suyūṭī interprets ʿUmar's request as asking permission or ability."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q53", "question": "What is the sūra's setting and thematic center in the cited overview?", "turns_on": "Iṣlāḥī disputes the received place-of-revelation classification.", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q53/p1", "position": "The sūra presents revelation and a conflict in which the useful truth is destined to prevail.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī describes the thunder/rain alternation of guidance and blindness; Iṣlāḥī connects it to the Prophet's preaching."}, {"id": "13:17/q53/p2", "position": "Al-Raʿd is wholly Makkan, with 13:17–22 as its thematic center.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī rejects the codices' Madinan classification; he contrasts Yūsuf's narrative argument with al-Raʿd's appeal to intellect and nature."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q54", "question": "What further teaching on scholarly effort is included?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q54/p1", "position": "Learning requires patience, breadth across disciplines, and deep mastery of one's specialty.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the seeker should take a valuable share from each science, master principles and branches, summarize them, and answer objections."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q55", "question": "What does the cited word ṭughyān mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q55/p1", "position": "Exceeding a limit, including a flood's swollen surge.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī applies it to disobedience, overflowing floodwater, surging seas, and flowing blood; al-Khalīl records ṭughyān/ṭughwān and two verb stems."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q56", "question": "What is said about Qurʾānic legal scholarship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q56/p1", "position": "Named scholars compiled legal studies of the Qurʾān by school.", "reasons": "Zarkashī lists al-Shāfiʿī first, al-Kiyā among Shāfiʿīs, al-Rāzī among Ḥanafīs, named Mālikīs, and Abū Yaʿlā among Ḥanbalīs."}]}
{"id": "13:17/q57", "question": "How does the Qurʾān relate to earlier scriptures?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:17/q57/p1", "position": "As final scripture it is self-sufficient and clarifies earlier books.", "reasons": "Zarkashī cites 27:76 on disputes of the Children of Israel."}]}
{"id": "15:73/q01", "question": "What does it mean that the cry seized them?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:73/q01/p1", "position": "It overpowered them and took control of them.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explains seizure as overpowering and control, and notes that akhīdh can mean a captive."}]}
{"id": "15:73/q02", "question": "Who were seized?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:73/q02/p1", "position": "The people of Lot.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī's commentators, al-Baghawī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Bursawī, Iṣlāḥī and Kur'an Yolu identify the afflicted people as Lot's people."}]}
{"id": "15:73/q03", "question": "What was the ṣayḥa that struck them?", "turns_on": "Whether the sound is identified with Gabriel, divine production, a thunderbolt, or a more general destructive blast; al-Rāzī and the Imam demand strong evidence for Gabriel's identification.", "positions": [{"id": "15:73/q03/p1", "position": "A tremendous, deadly cry or blast of punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Qurṭubī call it punishment; al-Jishumī defines ṣayḥa as a loud forceful sound. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it a sudden blast of impact unlike Thamud's, while Abū Ḥayyān reports his description as a cry of terror. Al-Bayḍāwī describes a terrifying deadly blast. Al-Biqāʿī says its force made other sounds negligible. Al-Ālūsī takes the definite article generically. Asad calls it a blast of God's punishment. Iṣlāḥī says it is a shout denoting punishment, aptly named for the storm wind's thunder and lightning. Kur'an Yolu calls it a terrible cry; al-Rāzī says the verse itself establishes only a tremendous deadly cry, absent strong external proof of Gabriel. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ surveys Qur'anic uses of ṣayḥa as an alarm cry at enemies, a destructive blast, and the resurrection call, citing examples across suras; the destructive blast is the sense relevant here."}, {"id": "15:73/q03/p2", "position": "It was Gabriel's cry or shout.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī's commentators, al-Wāḥidī's Wajīz, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Nasafī and al-Bursawī identify Gabriel; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Bayḍāwī report that identification. Al-Ālūsī reports that on this view the definite article points to a known event.
